implementation_notes: JavaScript is single-threaded per realm, so the whole synchronisation half of the pattern disappears: a closure variable plus the nullish coalescing assignment cached ??= build() (ES2021) replaces the marker-and-guard structure with one operator, and the assignment itself is atomic with respect to other tasks. The remaining hazard is yield-based re-entrancy: if the initialiser is asynchronous, the guard must cache the promise rather than the resolved value, otherwise two interleaved callers both build. The classic explicit flag/value cell is still justified when the value may legitimately be undefined (??= cannot distinguish it) or when the cell has to be reset.
pitfalls: `x ??= await build()` yields before assigning, so concurrent callers can run the initialiser several times and lose results - cache the promise (pending ??= load()) for asynchronous laziness.
??= treats only null/undefined as unset: a legitimately undefined result means the initialiser runs on every access (use a separate boolean/state field when undefined is a valid value).
Module-level memoisation is per realm: in worker threads, server-side per-request module instances or hot-reload scenarios each get their own cell, so 'once per process' assumptions do not hold.
Closure cells are invisible: a getter that hides a 200 ms build (or synchronous I/O such as reading a config file) makes the first call look like a hang to callers and profilers.

variants.name: Class getter over a #private field
variants.implementation_notes: Inside a class the same operator sits behind an accessor so the laziness is part of the type's API: a #private field holds the cell, the getter assigns on first read and the private name keeps the marker out of serialisation, logging and external mutation. Private fields (ES2022) also prevent the classic bug of a caller overwriting the cached value. Replacing the constructor-time build with this accessor is the whole change; an arrow-function class field initialiser would evaluate eagerly at construction and defeats it.
pitfalls: Class field initialisers (including arrow functions assigned to fields) run in the constructor: declaring `report = buildReport()` eagerly builds, and only the #private field plus accessor defers anything.

A getter that builds is invisible to `JSON.stringify`, spread and debugger inspection of the object, so profiling tools may trigger the expensive path merely by inspecting it - keep the build behind a method when the cost is I/O-bound.
Private-field laziness is per instance: cloning or deserialising an object creates a fresh empty cell (no sharing), which is safe but silently rebuilds per copy.
The getter is indistinguishable from a plain property to callers (it cannot be awaited), so an asynchronous build cannot live there - it must return a cached promise instead.

variants.name: Module-level laziness with dynamic import()
variants.implementation_notes: For module-scope laziness the cell holds a promise: import('./heavy.js') loads and evaluates the module on first use, and the module registry guarantees a single evaluation per specifier, so the memoised promise gives exactly-once semantics without any flag. This replaces both the eager top-level import (which makes startup pay for everything) and a hand-written require-cache. ESM's own laziness only extends as far as the module graph, so the dynamic form is the tool for genuinely optional or expensive submodules.
pitfalls: The memoised value is a promise: an import that fails is rejected, and the rejected promise is now cached, so a transient chunk-load failure (offline, network blip) stays failed until the cell is reset - clear the variable in a catch when retry matters.
Bundlers rewrite dynamic import specifiers, so a computed path (import(prefix + name)) can escape code splitting and pull the module back into the main bundle.
Module evaluation happens once per realm and is invisible to the caller: a 'lazy' import still blocks the first await, and its top-level side effects land at an unpredictable point in the program.
